chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from Muhammad ibn 'Isa ibn 'Ubayd from Yunus ibn 'Abd al-Rahman from Abu Basir and Sama'ah from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) regarding a group of people who fasted the month of Ramadan, and a black cloud covered them at sunset, so they thought it was night. He said: 'The one who broke his fast that day, indeed Allah, Exalted and Majestic, says: Then complete the fast until night. Whoever eats before night enters, upon him is its making up, because he ate deliberately. The aspect in this narration is that when one doubts the entry of night due to an occurrence (cloud), and his conjectures are equal and neither has an advantage over the other, it is not permissible for him to break his fast until he is certain of the entry of night or his conjecture prevails. And when he breaks his fast and the matter is as we described, making up is obligatory upon him according to what this news contains. As for when his conjection prevails that night has entered, so he breaks his fast, then it becomes clear afterwards that it had not entered, he should cease from eating and there is no making up upon him according to what the first news contained.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if I break my fast because I thought it was night but it wasn't yet?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Isfahaniyyah clarifies the jurisprudential distinction between doubt (shakk) and conviction (ghalabat al-zann) regarding the onset of night during Ramadan. It establishes that while mistaken conviction exempts one from making up the fast (qada), mere uncertainty requires it, reflecting the Shia principle of acting on the most probable opinion when evidence is balanced.
